newsitem.title: USA: Enron forms power joint venture with Italy's Enel.
newsitem.headline: Enron forms power joint venture with Italy's Enel.

text.p: Enron Corp. said Tuesday it will form a joint venture with Italy's Enel to take advantage of deregulation in the European electricity market, packing even more muscle onto two of the world's largest power companies.

The Houston-based utility's Enron Europe Ltd. subsidiary and Italy's state-owned L'Ente Nazionale per L'Energia Elettrica SpA, known as Enel, signed a non-binding letter of intent for the venture, each taking a $300 million equity stake.
The venture will own 5,000 megawatts of generating capacity, out of Enel's total capacity of 55,000 megawatts. Enron is expected to serve as fuel manager.
The venture will also raise $2.4 billion in debt finance.

Faced with pedestrian growth and uncertainty in the home electricity market, Enron and other U.S. power companies are turning to prospects offered by deregulation in Europe, just as they snapped up assets in Britain in the 1990s.

The European Union's electricity liberalisation programme takes effect in 1999, and new generators will be allowed to compete for 30 percent of the European Union market, a slice worth some $50 billion a year.

"We have had the experience of deregulation in U.S. power markets and in Britain, now we are seeing Europe move down the same road and we are well positioned to be a part of that," said a spokeswoman for Enron.
Enron's move comes just three weeks after Southern Co. and its German partner, Veba AG, agreed to pay $1.7 billion for the Berliner Kraft und Licht AG, which supplies power to the city of Berlin.

The planned deal marks the second time in a month that Enel has decided to dispose of a chunk of its existing 55,000-megawatt power network in preparation for the opening of the Italian electricity distribution market in 1999.
With over 650,000 miles of transmission lines, Enel is the world's second-largest electric utility in terms of installed power and number of customers. It has 90,600 employees.
Some analysts, however, question whether independent power producers such as Enron or utilities such as Southern are going to find it so easy to penetrate the European market.
"U.S. power producers are paying quite a high price for companies which are just about to go into a more extreme form of competition," said Simon Allen, a consultant at Price Waterhouse in London.

Unlike in Britain, where the electricity market had been derergulated when U.S. power companies started their buying spree, Europe faces a long road to liberalisation and government companies are unlikely to surrender their role easily.
Analysts also note the transmission lines which connect European countries are designed to provide backup power, not to create an integrated market.

"It is not as if these European companies will not have thought of this, they are not going to surrender market share to Enron, they will do it themselves," said Chris Rogers, analyst at Union Bank of Switzerland in London.

Indeed, Enron could be placed in the position of building gas-fired plants to feed cheap electricity into the government or monopoly system and in effect subsidise the closure of more expensive European coal- or oil-fired capacity.

Even within the Italian market, Enron may face problems because Enel already has a deal to build natural gas-fired power stations with national oil company Ente Nazionale Idrocarburi SpA (ENI) and it is difficult to see ENI giving way to Enron.

Joint ventures may be the only way for U.S. companies to achieve a role in Continental Europe, but they are likely to grab a market share of 5 percent to 7 percent, rather than the 10 percent or 20 percent they hope for, analysts said.

Some analysts question whether Enron will be willing to take such a pittance, since the company is known to seek only the top power project in any one country and has walked away from the deal which Southern struck with Bewag.
"One also has to question whether with so many projects on the books, a company like Enron has the brainpower to keep all these things going at once," said one analyst.
Enron's stock rose 50 cents to $40.50 in consolidated trading on the New York Stock Exchange.
